content: The circumcision procedure, regardless of the method used for Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC), should be accompanied by comprehensive education for individuals and communities on proper wound care following circumcision or any other surgical procedure. This is essential to ensure optimal healing and prevent complications. To mitigate the risk of tetanus associated with VMMC services, the Uganda Ministry of Health mandates that all VMMC sites include tetanus vaccination as part of their service package. This can be achieved through mass vaccination campaigns during demand creation and mobilization efforts or by administering tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines (TTCV) to men without a prior history of tetanus immunization. The Ministry of Health, along with implementing partners, has developed various resources to support the integration of tetanus risk mitigation into VMMC services. These resources include site readiness assessment tools and informational materials for both providers and clients. The introduction of TTCV for VMMC is relevant only in countries implementing VMMC programs, such as Botswana, Ethiopia, Kenya, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Rwanda, South Africa, Swaziland, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. However, in other countries where traditional circumcision ceremonies are practiced, efforts should still be made to protect populations from tetanus. The provision of multiple TTCV doses throughout the life course offers numerous opportunities for integration with other health services. For instance, the introduction of the HPV vaccine could serve as an opportunity to offer TTCV to both males and females. Additionally, adolescent health services, including education on safe sexual practices to prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, could be provided concurrently where appropriate. Hygiene kits, which may include items such as cooking sets, soap, buckets, water purification tablets, and jerry cans, are critical in addressing diseases caused by inadequate hygiene. Safe water and proper sanitation are fundamental to health. The distribution of hygiene kits presents an opportunity to reach individuals of all ages and can be integrated with hygiene promotion, water improvement activities, emergency responses, or routine immunization programs. For example, in Kenya, a study demonstrated that distributing hygiene kits during routine immunizations positively impacted household water treatment and hygiene practices without negatively affecting vaccination coverage. Hearing impairment in children poses a significant barrier to their optimal development and education. Routine immunization visits have been utilized as opportunities to conduct infant hearing screenings. Studies from Nigeria and South Africa have shown that integrating hearing screening with immunization visits enables the early detection of hearing loss. In Nigeria, where only BCG vaccination visits were used, 88% of infants under three months of age were screened. In South Africa, where all infant vaccination visits were utilized, 93% of infants under 12 months of age were screened. Early detection of hearing loss is critical, with the benchmark for confirmation being under three months of age. Hearing screening conducted during immunization visits at younger ages, such as during BCG or DTP1 vaccinations, facilitates earlier identification of hearing loss. The integration of immunization services with other health interventions throughout the life course provides a valuable opportunity to enhance public health outcomes. This approach requires careful planning, resource allocation, and monitoring to ensure the effectiveness and acceptance of integrated services.
